items.title: Nat Hentoff interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007
items.q: I knew him first because he played with Max Roach

ctx.x: That’s good. When they’d improvise these blues then you’d have to name it something, right?

They’d name it. See one other thing is, the leader of the date was always at the final session, the final cutting session. It was his recording. I wasn’t going to say what tracks we’re going to use etcetera. And you know for example one of the things I was most pleased to do, because the guy died so young, Booker Little. He wrote most of the music, he played trumpet on it, and it was just amazing stuff. You know I knew him first because he played with Max Roach, but he had, talk about knowing a person’s sound, he…

items.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: when Max Roach was saying to me, jazz is very much like the Constitution in action.

ctx.x: In a sense in a very jazz-improvisatory kind of way, being open to the moment.

Yeah, but also, the more I got into the Constitution – years later, when Max Roach was saying to me, jazz is very much like the Constitution in action. Here are these individual people, very attentive to all of the other individuals who are playing and collectively they create something bigger than themselves.
To go back to Boston Latin just for one quick moment: was that an integrated school? Were there black students?
